Two broad categories of sources help reconstruct Kakatiya history: **Archaeological** and **Literary**.

**Archaeological sources** — Inscriptions, coins, and monuments.

*   Inscriptions give information on socio-economic conditions, wars, conquests, and military affairs of the period.
*   Gold, silver, and copper coins were minted; **Kesari Gaddyana, Nishka, Madas, and Kesaris and Pati-Varas** are the important coin types.
*   Kakatiya monuments include the **Orugallu fort**, the famous **Kakatiya Toranas** (entrance arches), the **thousand-pillar temple at Anumakonda**, the **Ramappa temple at Palampet**, and other temples at **Pillalamarri, Nagulapadu, and Ghanapuram**. Sculptures on the walls, pillars, and doors of these temples reflect the drapery and ornament styles of the period, and some important events are carved as panels on temple walls.

**Key inscriptions and what they reveal:**

| Inscription | Issued by | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Magallu inscription (A.D. 956) | Eastern Chalukyan king Danarnava | First mention of Kakartya Gundyana and his preceding generations |
| Anumakonda 1000-pillar temple inscription (A.D. 1163) | Rudradeva | Declaration of independence |
| Draksharamam temple inscription (A.D. 1158) | Prola II's minister Inangala Brahmireddy | Records Prola II's son Rudradeva's accession |
| Bayyaram inscription (A.D. 1219) | Ganapatideva's sister Mailamba | Digging of Bayyaram tank (Khammam district) |
| Motupalli inscription (A.D. 1244) | Ganapatideva | Remissions granted to foreign merchants |
| Malkapuram inscription (A.D. 1261) | Ganapatideva | References to Vidyamandapas (educational institutions) |
| Chandupatla inscription (A.D. 1289) | Rudramadevi's servant Puvvulamummadi | Rudramadevi's death while suppressing Ambadeva's revolt |
| Tripurantakam inscription (Nellore) (A.D. 1291) | Ambadeva, Rudrama's official | Records Ambadeva's victories |
| Salakalaveedu inscription (A.D. 1317) | Pratapa Rudra II | Donation marking victory over the Pandyas |
| Kolunupalli inscription (Mahaboobnagar) (A.D. 1321) | Pratapa Rudra II | Donations to Chenna Keshavaswamy and Narasimhaswamy temples |

**Literary sources** are equally important, written in Telugu, Sanskrit, and other languages:

| Book | Author | Language | Details |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pandiradya Charitam, Basavapuranam | Palkuriki Somanatha | Telugu | Conditions of Saivism and other religions |
| Neetisaram / Neeti Sastramuktavali | Baddena | Telugu | Explains Raja neeti and Raja dharma |
| Shivayogasaram | Kolanu Ganapatideva | Telugu | History of Indaluri Nayakas |
| Kridhabhiramam | Venukonda Vallabharaya | Telugu | Life and conditions of people in Warangal fort |
| Pratapa­rudriyam (Pratapa­rudra Yashobhushanam) | Vidyanatha | Sanskrit | Written by Pratapa Rudra II's court poet |
| Nrutyarathnavali | Jayapa Senani | Sanskrit | Characteristics of Nrutya and Natya |
| Andhra Mahabharatam | Tikkana Somayaji | Telugu | Written at Ganapatideva's court, at friend Manumasiddi's request |
| Nirvachanottara Ramayanam | Tikkana Somayaji | Telugu | Viraata Parvam |

Contemporaries writing in other languages also inform Kakatiya history: **Tariq-i-Farishta** (Farishta), **Futuh-us-Salatin** (Isami), **Tariq-i-Ferozshahi** (Barani), **Rehalla** (Ibn Battuta), and **"The Travels"** by Marco Polo, who recorded details of foreign trade at Motupalli during Rudramadevi's period.

The identity and early history of the Kakatiyas is drawn mainly from inscriptions and literary works.

The Eastern Chalukyan king Danarnava's **Magallu inscription (A.D. 956)** is the earliest to mention Kakartya Gundyana along with his preceding three generations. Some historians regard him as the founder of the dynasty.

There is no unanimity on the origin of the name "Kakatiya":

*   One group holds that **Kakatipuram** village was their early home, and the family took its name from this place.
*   A second group holds that the Kakatiyas worshipped **'Kakati,'** a local mother goddess (originally a Jain goddess), and derived their name from her.
    *   Kumaraswamy Somapeethi, a 15th-century commentator on Vidyanatha's Pratapa­rudriya, states that the family took the name Kakatiya because they worshipped Kakati, considered one of the forms of goddess Durga.
    *   Vinukonda Vallabharaya's Kridhabhiramam also mentions the idol of the Kakati goddess.
    *   Sitabkhan's 16th-century inscription records that Sitabkhan reinstated the Kakati idol in Warangal fort after it was destroyed by the Delhi Sultanate's army.
*   Kakati is not named among Durga's forms in the Hindu puranas, but many village goddesses were locally accepted as forms of Durga — so Kakati came to be worshipped this way, alongside the village goddess Ekaveera.

The early members of the family are described as **feudatory Kakatiyas**. From Kakartya Gundyana to Rudra I (Rudradeva) — that is, from A.D. 956 to 1162 — the rulers of present-day Karimnagar, Warangal, and Khammam were feudatories, first serving the Rashtrakutas and later the Kalyana Chalukyas.

Kakartya Gundyana played a crucial role in the conquest of Bezavada fort under the **Rashtrakuta king Krishna II** but lost his life in the Peruvangooru battle against the Vengi Chalukyas. Impressed by his feudatory's faithfulness, the Rashtrakuta emperor appointed Gundyana's son **Eriya** as administrator of Kurivadi (Warangal) seema, which was earlier under the Mudigonda Chalukyas. This appointment marked the beginning of Kakatiya rule and relations with the people of Telangana.

### Betaraja I

When Kakartya Gundyana died, Beta I was a small child, and protection of the kingdom fell to his maternal aunt Kamasani and her husband, **Veeriyala Errabhupati**. Errabhupati reinstated Beta I at Kakatipuram after defeating his enemies and expanded his rule to Koraviseema.

*   After Errabhupati's death, Beta faced renewed danger from the Vengi Chalukyas.
*   On Kamasani's advice, Beta accepted the **Kalyana Chalukya king as his overlord**, and with Chalukya support was able to face the Vengi threat.
*   Beta I held the title **"Kakatipuradhinatha."**

### Prolaraja I (A.D. 1050–1075)

Son of Betaraja I. His achievements are recorded in the Khajipeta, Pillalamarri, and Palampeta inscriptions.

**Conquests:**

*   Set right the chakrakuta; conquered the Konkana Mandala.
*   Killed Gonaaraja of Purukuta.
*   Defeated the Bhadranagapuradeeshvara (ruler near the Indravati River) and killed the Purukuta king in battle.
*   Defeated Kodavarti Duggaraju (ruling near Warangal) and occupied his territory.

**Status:** Kalyana Chalukya king Someshvara I, appreciating Prolaraja I's achievements, appointed him feudatory ruler of Anumakonda Vishaya with hereditary rights — a recognition that enhanced Prola I's status even though Anumakonda was already under his rule.

Most of Prolaraja I's victories are tied to his overlord's campaigns. According to Bilhana's Vikramankadeva Charitra, Someshvara I sent an army under his son Vikramaditya to conquer the Chola kingdom; this army moved through Konkan, Kerala, and the Pandya kingdoms to Gangaikondapuram and Kanchipuram, and then to Vengi and Chakrakuta. Prola I fought in the Konkana, Gangaikonda, and Kanchi campaigns and, after the overlord's army moved to Chakrakuta, took charge there himself.

### Betaraja II (A.D. 1075–1108)

Son and successor of Prolaraja I.

*   His **Anumakonda inscription** (A.D. 1070–80) does not mention the title "Tribhuvanamalla," but his **Khajipeta inscription** of A.D. 1090 mentions this title along with another — "Vikramachakriya."
*   During this period there was fierce enmity between the Chola Chalukyas and Kalyana Chalukyas; to occupy Vengi, Vikramaditya likely sought Betaraja's help. Betaraja's minister Vaizadandanatha played an important role in this.
*   Pleased with the help in conquering Vengi, Vikramaditya VI handed over Sabbi Mandala to Betaraja, enhancing his status.
*   Betaraja II took titles including **Mahamandaleshvara, Tribhubanamalla, and Vikramachakri.**
*   His spiritual master (guru) was **Rameshwara Deekshitha**.
*   On Beta II's death in A.D. 1108, his son **Durgarupati** ascended the throne.

### Prolaraja II (A.D. 1115–1157)

The strongest ruler among the feudatory Kakatiyas, ascending the throne after his brother Durgaraju.

**Military achievements:**

*   Immediately after ascending, defeated the feudatory rulers of Kalyana Chalukyas on his kingdom's borders — a fact supported by his son Rudradeva's Thousand Pillar Temple inscription at Anumakonda.
*   Defeated **Paramara Jaggadeva**, ruler of Kolanupaka.
*   In **A.D. 1137**, together with his friend, Kalyana Chalukya king **Jagadekamalla II**, attacked and defeated the army of the Kanduri Chodas, killing their king Tailapa (who had earlier defeated Bheema Choda).
*   Marched to Srisailam and erected a pillar of victory there.
*   Made war with Rajendra Chola.

**Relations with the Polavasa lords:** Friction developed between the Polavasa lords and the Kakatiyas — though both were feudatories of the Kalyana Chalukyas, family feuds over inheritance repeatedly put them on opposite (and sometimes the same) sides.

**Significance:** Prolaraja II successfully checked the declining influence of the Kalyana Chalukyas in Telangana and made the Kakatiyas a strong regional force.

**End:** Prolaraja II was killed by enemy forces. He was succeeded by his son **Rudradeva**, who ascended the throne in **A.D. 1158**, remained a feudatory until **A.D. 1162**, and then declared independence.

Rudradeva, who ascended the throne in A.D. 1158 as a feudatory of the Kalyana Chalukyas, **declared independence in 1163**, as recorded in the Thousand Pillar Temple inscription of Anumakonda. From this point the Kakatiyas ruled as sovereigns.

The independent Kakatiya rulers, in order, were:

| Ruler | Reign |
|---|---|
| Rudradeva | A.D. 1163–1195 |
| Mahadeva | A.D. 1195–1199 |
| Ganapatideva | A.D. 1199–1262 |
| Rudramadevi | A.D. 1262–1289 |
| Pratapa Rudra II | A.D. 1289–1323 |

They ruled with Warangal as their capital for about **160 years**, uniting the Telugu-speaking people under one banner and doing unique service to Telugu culture — earning permanent fame in the medieval history of Telangana and Dakshinapatha. The Sovereign Kakatiyas fought against contemporary Hindu kingdoms — the Yadavas, Hoyasalas, and Pandyas — and their rule finally ended with the attacks of the Delhi Sultans.

### Rudradeva (A.D. 1158–1195)

Rudradeva's reign falls into two phases: **feudatory (A.D. 1158–1163)** and **independent (A.D. 1163–1195)**. His mother was Muppamamba and father was Prola II. His minister Inangala Brahmireddy's Draksharamam inscription describes him as a great warrior; Chalukya-Chola king Raja Raja II was his contemporary, and in this inscription he is called "Anumakonda Rudra."

**Conquests and expansion:**

*   Defeated the rulers of Nagar (Karimnagar/Naganuru) — Dommaraja, Polavasa ruler Medaraju II, Myligadeva, and Chodo Udaya — establishing dominance over Telangana.
*   Rudradeva first defeated **Mylagideva** and then attacked the Kalachuris; after occupying the Kalachuri kingdom, his territory extended north to the banks of the Godavari, and Sabbinadu also came under Kakatiya control.
*   **Marched against the Kanduri Chodas**: after Tailapdeva's death, his successors Kanduri Choda Bheema (capital at Vardhamanapura) and Kanduri Udayachoda contested the throne at Panugallu. Rudradeva took the opportunity, conquered the Kanduri kingdom, and merged it into his own — appointing Udayachoda as his feudatory and marrying his daughter Padmavati.
*   The A.D. 1202 **Jammaluru inscription** of Cheruku Bollayya records that Rudradeva handed over the vast forest area of Srisailam to his friend Cheruku Bollayya. Through these victories, his influence extended to today's Nalgonda and Mahaboobnagar areas, and his kingdom's boundary reached the Godavari in the north, Bidar in the west, and Srisailam in the south.
*   Issued a **Vijaya Sasana** (victory inscription) at Anumakonda and built a temple there consecrating the idols of Rudreshvara, Vasudeva, and Suryadeva.
*   Declared war ("Palanati war") on those responsible for his father's death, aiding Nalagamaraju; around the same time the Chalukyas of Pithapuram sought his friendship. He also planned to occupy the Velanati Choda kingdom, attacking their feudatory Kondapadamatis (supported by the Tripuranthakam inscription).
*   Fought the Yadavas while trying to expand westward; in the **A.D. 1195 war with Yadava king Jaitugi (Jaitrapala)**, the Kakatiya army was defeated and **Rudradeva lost his life**.

**Rudradeva's greatness and administration:**

*   Established sovereign Kakatiya power with **Warangal as capital.**
*   His most able administrator was **Gangadhara of the Vellanki family** (inscription from Karimnagar, A.D. 1170), who joined as army chief under Prola II, administered Anumakonda, and later, under Rudradeva, excavated a water tank and built the Prasanna Keshava swamy temple at Anumakonda.
*   Built the **Thousand Pillar Temple**; built, near Anumakonda, a new city for civil and military convenience — **Warangal (Orugallu) fort**, which became the new Kakatiya capital.
*   A great patron of arts, poets, and literature — called "**Kalpa taruvu**" (wish-fulfilling tree) to scholars, per the Nayareddy Pillalamarri inscription of A.D. 1196.
*   The Draksharamam inscription calls him "**Vinayabhusana**." In a poem in Baddena's Neetisaramuktavali, Rudradeva is named the author of Neetisastra.
*   Rudradeva was **childless** and was succeeded by his brother **Mahadeva in A.D. 1195** (supported by the Khandavalli copper plates).

### Mahadeva (A.D. 1155–1199, reign ~1195–1199)

Son of Prolaraja II and elder among Rudradeva's brothers. Very little inscriptional or literary information survives about him — two inscriptions: one from Sundela village, Peddapalli taluqa of Karimnagar (A.D. 1197), and a damaged, undated one from Warangal fort.

*   Fought only one war in his life — against the Yadavas — and was defeated and killed in it.
*   In the war with the Yadavas, Yadava king Jaitrapala defeated the "Trilingadhipati" (Mahadeva), based on the Paithan copper plates of Yadava Ramachandradeva, and then released young Ganapatideva from prison and placed him on the Warangal throne. This is also supported by literary works like Pratapa Charitra and Somadeva rajiyam.
*   During his period a feudatory ruler rebelled against him.
*   His queen was **Bayyamba**; they had a son, Ganapatideva, and two daughters, Mailamba and Kundamamba.
*   Mahadeva was a follower of Saivism; his teacher was Dhruveshwara Pandita.
*   His ablest army chief, **Recherla Rudra**, acted cleverly to protect Kakatiya rule when the kingdom was in crisis after the defeat by the Yadavas.

### Ganapatideva (A.D. 1199–1262)

Regarded as the greatest of the Kakatiya rulers, Ganapatideva's father died in the war with Jaitugi, and young Ganapatideva became a prisoner. With efforts made by Recherla Rudra, Jaitugi released Ganapatideva and had him anointed to the throne (A.D. 1199), and Ganapatideva then worked to suppress internal rebellions and enemies such as Mallyala Chounda.

Ganapatideva united all Telugu-speaking people and ruled efficiently for **63 years (A.D. 1199–1262)**, administering both Telangana and Andhra regions from his capital, Warangal. His first surviving inscription belonging to his reign is the **Manthena inscription** from Karimnagar, issued 26 December 1199.

**Why was Ganapatideva released?** Historians hold differing opinions:

1.  Many historians believe Hoyasala king Ballala II intended to take advantage of the situation at Warangal to expand his own kingdom; since this would raise Hoyasala prestige, the Yadavas — their strong rivals — did not want this, and so Jaitugi released young Ganapatideva to occupy the Warangal throne, checking Hoyasala expansion. This is viewed by these historians as a political move by the Yadavas.
2.  Moreover, Jaitugi gave his daughter **Somaladevi** in marriage to Ganapatideva.

**Kakatiya-Yadava contemporary rulers table:**

| King | Dynasty | Reign | Relation to Kakatiyas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jaitugi (Jaitrapala) | Yadavas (Devagiri) | A.D. 1193–1199 | Ganapatideva's father died fighting him |
| Singhana | Yadavas | A.D. 1200–1247 | War with Hoyasalas, victory |
| Krishana | Yadavas | A.D. 1246–1261 | — |
| Mahadeva | Yadavas | A.D. 1261–1271 | War with Hoyasalas |
| Ramachandradeva | Yadavas | A.D. 1271–1311 | War with Hoyasalas and defeat; later defeated by Delhi Sultans, accepted subordination |
| Shankera deva | Yadavas | A.D. 1311–1313 | Attacked and killed by Mallik Kafur |
| Harapala | Yadava | A.D. 1313–1317 | Defeated and killed by Alauddin Khilji's son Mubarak Shah; downfall of Yadava kingdom |

**Kakatiya-Hoyasala contemporary rulers table:**

| King | Reign | Relation to Kakatiyas |
|---|---|---|
| Bhallala II | A.D. 1170–1220 | Defeat of Yadava king Billalmadeva |
| Narasimha II | A.D. 1220–1254 | — |
| Narasimha III | A.D. 1254–1295 | War with Yadava Ramachandradeva (victory); defeated by Pandya king Kulashekara |
| Bhallala III | A.D. 1295–1342 | Attacked Yadava kingdom (A.D. 1305), defeated Ramachandra's army |

**Coastal conquests and expansion (from A.D. 1201):** By the time Ganapatideva ascended the throne, the older ruling families of the coastal region — Eastern Chalukyas, Chola-Chalukyas, Kalyana Chalukyas — had grown weak. The **Velanati kingdom** was powerful; its ruler **Prudhvishwara** (grandson of Chola Rajendra II) had made neighbouring rulers his feudatories, including the Kolanu kings (Kolleru), Kotas of Guntur, Prakasham Konidena Telugu Cholas (Nellore, Kadapa, Chengalpattu), Gudimetta Chagis (Krishna bank), and Natavadi kings (Khammam district), with some coastal areas under the Kalinga Gangas.

*   Ganapatideva invaded the coastal region in A.D. 1201; the **Bezavada inscription** (A.D. 1201, issued by Nattavadi Rudra, Ganapatideva's brother-in-law) records his army's victory over Prudhvishwara's forces, and the Kota Nayakas of Dharani Kota were made feudatories.
*   He then invaded **Divi Seema**, ruled by the Ayyavamsha rulers. Their ruler **Pinna Choda** fought fiercely but was defeated; Ganapatideva's army chief **Malyala Chounda** took the titles "Dwipiluntaka" and "Divichoorakaara" for this conquest.
*   As a political strategy, Ganapatideva handed Divi Seema **back** to Pinna Choda, securing support for further expansion; this led to matrimonial ties — Ayyavamsha Pinnachoda gave his two daughters, **Naramba and Peramba**, in marriage to Ganapatideva, and Pinnachoda's son **Jaayapa** was appointed **Gajashahini** in the Kakatiya army.
*   With the Ayyavamshas as feudatories, Prudhvishwara's strength weakened further; Nellore's Tikkaraju and others also joined Ganapatideva's side. **Prudhvishwara lost his life in the war** — Ganapatideva's inscriptions describe him as having "played with Prudhvishwara's head as a ball" (_prudhvishwara shirah kanduka kreeda vinodah_). The last Ayyavamsha inscription (from Anantha, treasurer of Prudhvishwara, A.D. 1206) suggests Prudhvishwara died in defeat around this time. Ganapatideva appointed **Jayapa Senani as viceroy** of this region.

**Southern conquests (A.D. 1207–1209):** Ganapatideva waged two southern expeditions, driven by the contemporary political situation of the **Telugu Chodas of Nellore**.

*   Telugu Choda king **Nallasiddi** had declared Nellore's independence taking advantage of a weakening Chola emperor Rajadhiraja II. His successors — Betaraja I, Errasiddi (with sons Manumasiddi I and Tammasiddi) — followed.
*   Chola emperor Kulathonga III interfered in Telugu Choda politics: when Manumasiddi I ascended, Kulothunga III invaded Nellore and defeated him, then handed the Nellore throne back to Nallasiddi as his feudatory.
*   Later, Manumasiddi I's son **Tikka Bhupala** sought Ganapatideva's help against Tammasiddi. Ganapatideva's army invaded the Nellore Choda kingdom (**A.D. 1207–1208**), defeated Tammasiddi, and installed Tikkabhupala as ruler of Nellore — supported by the Chebrolu inscription (A.D. 1228) and Jayapasenani's Ganpeshwaram inscription (A.D. 1231). This was Ganapatideva's first southern victory; his army also attacked **Kanchi**, the Chola capital.

**Kalinga conquest (A.D. 1211–1212):** After the Velanadu and Nellore victories, Ganapatideva sent his armies to Kalinga (earlier under Prudhvishwara). Army chief **Induluri Somaya mantri** led the campaign; Kalinga king **Aniyanka Bheema III** faced the Kakatiya army, but neither side was decisively victorious. Ganapatideva made matrimonial alliances instead: he married his elder daughter **Ganapaamba** to Kota Rudra's son Myna Beta, and his second daughter **Rudramadevi** to Needadavolu Chalukya king Veerabhadra. Later, under Aniyanka Bheema's son Narasimhadeva, the Kakatiya army attacked and conquered Vengi and Kalinga again (A.D. 1238).

**Later career and Muthukuru defeat:**

*   In A.D. 1248, Ganapatideva's friend Choda Tikkaraju died; his son Manumasidde II (Veera Ganda Gopala) lost his kingdom to rival kinsmen and sent his minister-poet Tikkana Somayaji to Ganapatideva's court for help. Ganapatideva sent an army under **Samantha Bhoja**, defeated Manumasiddi's enemies Bayyana and Akkana, occupied Kanchi (capital of Kulothunga/Rajendra III Chola), and later defeated a combined Dravida-Karnataka army at Palleyuru in Tanjore district. By A.D. 1250, Manumasiddi II was reinstalled at Nellore.
*   Kakatiya army also defeated Vaidumba king Rakkasi Gangadi, with Kayastha **Gangaya Sayani** (Manumasiddi's army chief) participating. Ganapatideva returned the occupied kingdom and recognized Gangaya Sayani's capability, appointing him **Bahattar Niyogadhipati** (supervisor over the seventy-two Niyogas) — supported by the Tripurantakam inscription of A.D. 1250.
*   **Kakatiya–Yadava relations** remained friendly under contemporary Yadava king Singhana; no war is recorded between them. Yadava king Singhana's son Permadideva reportedly lived at Ganapatideva's court for a period.
*   **War with Pandya king Jataverman Sundar Pandya (A.D. 1257–1263):** By A.D. 1257, Sundar Pandya invaded the Nellore Telugu Choda kingdom, which had earlier accepted his overlordship; Manumasiddi II sought help from the Kakatiya, Yadava, and Bana kings.

*    The Pandya king split his army into two divisions — one against Draksharamam (defeated by the Kakatiya army, with its commander Koppera Zingana accepting Ganapatideva's overlordship), and a second against Manumasiddi II at Nellore. By **A.D. 1263**, the Pandya army reached Muthukuru near Nellore; in the fierce battle, the Kakatiya army and its allies were **defeated** — Veera Ganda Gopala lost his life and Manumasiddi died. Nellore became part of the Pandya kingdom. 
*   This was the **only defeat** in Ganapatideva's 62-year career, and it led him to hand over administration to his daughter **Rudramadevi**.

**Importance of Ganapatideva:** A great emperor and political strategist, he saved the Kakatiya kingdom from internal disturbances, rebellions, and external attacks; strengthened his power through matrimonial alliances and diplomacy; transferred the capital from Anumakonda to Warangal; and completed the construction of the new capital city Orugallu, begun by his grandfather Prola and uncle Rudradeva. 

*   His feudatories and army chiefs included Recherla Rudra, the Malyala Nayakas (Malyala Choda and his son Katama), Jayapa of Divi Seema (Gajasahini), Nellore's Manumasiddi (a good friend), Induluri Somaya mantri, Prolabhima Nayaka, and Kayastha Gangaya Sahini.

Rudramadevi is considered one of the most meritorious administrators in the history of medieval India, especially South India. Daughter of Somamba and Ganapatideva, she was trained under her father's supervision in political administration and army affairs. Since Ganapatideva had no sons, he declared her his successor and handed over administration to her in **A.D. 1262**, after his defeat at Muthukuru.

**Marco Polo's account:** The Venetian traveller Marco Polo visited India during Rudramadevi's period, landing at the **Motupalli port**. He praised her administrative capabilities highly, along with the trade and commerce, export and import activity at the port, the conduct of port officials, and the care taken of foreign traders under her arrangements.

### Administration and Rebellions

When Rudramadevi took over administration, Kakatiya power was already under strain. Main causes: rebellion of feudatories and administrators, the defeat by the Pandyas at Muthukuru, and the threat of the Yadava king Mahadeva (A.D. 1262–1271), who planned to occupy Kakatiya territory.

*   During this critical period, **Recherla Prasadaditya** took responsibility for protecting the kingdom; the Velugoti Vanshavali records him with titles like "Kakatiya vamsha sthapanacharya" and "Rayapithamahanka."
*   Other loyal officials who stood guard for Rudramadevi included Kayastha Jennigadeva, Kayastha Tripurari, Malyala Gundiya Nayaka, and Madaya Nayaka, and Mahapradhana Kandara Nayaka.
*   According to Ekamranatha's Pratapa Charitra, her step-brothers **Harihara and Murari deva rebelled** against her; she suppressed these rebellions with the support of her able army chiefs.
*   Eastern Ganga king **Narasimha deva** invaded and occupied the Vengi kingdom. 

*   In **A.D. 1274**, his son **Bhanudeva I** invaded the Kakatiya kingdom; Rudramadevi's army chiefs **Potinayaka and Proli nayaka** defeated this invasion — a fact supported by the Draksharamam temple inscription.
*   The **Godavari River became the border** between the Kakatiya and Ganga kingdoms afterward.

### Yadava Invasion on the Kakatiya Kingdom

While Rudramadevi was suppressing internal rebellions, Yadava king Mahadeva invaded. She personally faced the Yadava army and won a decisive victory, driving the enemy back to the **Devagiri fort**. Her army chief **Sindhu Bhairava** played an important role in this war (recorded in an inscription found at Bidar fort).

*   A recently found inscription from **Allapadu** records that Yadava king Ellanadeva married Rudramadevi's daughter.
*   Hemadri, in his work "Vratakhandam," deliberately did not mention that his lord (the Yadava king) was defeated at the hands of a woman.
*   As a symbol of this historic victory, Rudramadevi took the title **"RayaGaja kesari"** and constructed the Ranga mandapam at the Swayambhu temple in Warangal fort. The title Rayagaja Kesari is also mentioned in her Bidar fort inscription.

### Rebellion of the Kayastha Ambadeva

The most serious challenge of her reign came in its final years from Kayastha **Ambadeva**, recorded in the Tripuranthakam and Nandaluru inscriptions.

*   Kayastha **Jennigadeva** was Rudramadevi's most faithful subordinate, ruling the Nandluru region (Kadapa district); on her orders, in A.D. 1264 he ended Pandya administration there.
*   After Jennigadeva, his younger brother **Tripuranthaka** ruled the region (A.D. 1270–1272), remaining faithful to Rudramadevi.
*   After Tripuranthaka, his younger brother **Ambadeva** became ruler of the region — but he **rejected Rudramadevi's subordination and rebelled**, defeated her feudatories, and made them his own subordinates. He allied with her enemies, the Pandyas and Yadavas.
*   According to the Tripuranthakam inscription (A.D. 1290), Ambadeva took titles including "Pandya rajanya-priya-preshita-chandavedanda-Turugasthaara-viraajmaana-samshoshita-souhaardra" and "Devagiri-rajaprasarpita-praabhrutamani-kanakabhushana."
*   Ambadeva defeated Rudramadevi's regent in the Guntur region, **Sripati Ganapati**, in A.D. 1273, taking the title **"Raya Sahasra malla,"** and occupied Valluru (under Pandya rule).
*   By A.D. 1287, Ambadeva occupied **Gandikota, Mulikinadu, Renadu, Perakallu, Sakilinadu, and Pottapinadu**, ruling from Vallura as capital (recorded in the Attirala inscription).

### Death of Rudramadevi

Ambadeva's expansion in all directions posed a grave danger to Rudramadevi's power. In **A.D. 1286, Ambadeva defeated the Pandyas**; the defeated Pandya king Maraverman Kulashekara fled the battlefield, and Ambadeva grew stronger.

Ambadeva's own Tripuranthakam inscription describes his victories. According to the recently found inscription at **Chandupatla village (Nalgonda district)**, **Rudramadevi and her chief Mallikarjuna rayalu lost their lives while suppressing Ambadeva's rebellion**. Mallikarjuna's servant Puvvalamummadi donated lands to the Somanatha temple in Chandupatla village to commemorate this.

The Chandupatla inscription does not give details of when or where Rudramadevi actually died — even today there is no complete historical source establishing the exact circumstances of her death. The majority view among historians is that she died before **27 November 1289**, while suppressing Ambadeva's rebellion, since no inscription of hers is found later than that date.

### Greatness of Rudramadevi

Rudramadevi ruled very efficiently from Orugallu as capital. Though a woman, she received thorough training in administrative affairs under her father's supervision and conducted governance with the welfare of the people as her aim. She faced enemy attacks daringly and had faithful, able army chiefs and feudatories who stood with her. Her only failure was the Ambadeva rebellion.

*   Among her army chiefs and feudatories: **Malyala, Recherla, Gona family, Reddy Nayakulu, and Velama families.** Among the Velama families, **Recherla Prasaditya** earned particular fame during her period. The **Kayastha kings**, who ruled prior to Ambadeva's rebellion, protected the south-western region of the kingdom from enemy attacks.
*   Her husband was **Chalukya Veerabhadra** of the Nidadavolu branch. Among her employees, Devagiri king Singhana's son **Sarangapani** was important; **Ranaka Gopadevaraju** of the 'Are' community was also in her service.
*   Rudramadevi had **three daughters**: **Mummadamma, Rudrama, and Ruyyamma**. Since she had no son, her daughter Mummadamma's son **Pratapa Rudra II** was declared her successor. Mummadamma's husband was Mahadeva, a Kakatiya prince. Her second daughter married the Yadava prince Ellanadeva. Her youngest daughter's husband was Induluri nayaka.
*   In the medieval history of the Deccan, Rudramadevi ruled prior to Chanda Bibi and Hayat Bakshi Begum, and earned lasting fame among them.

The last ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty. Prior to Ambadeva's rebellion, Rudramadevi had already declared Pratapa Rudra II as her successor. He took over the administration in **A.D. 1290**, ruling with two main aims: **1)** to finish off the danger arising from Ambadeva's rebellion, and **2)** to protect the Kakatiya kingdom from enemy attacks.

**Army reorganization:** To fulfil these aims, Pratapa Rudra II overhauled the army, handing control to the **Nayakas** — he appointed **77 Nayakas**, explained to them how many soldiers each needed to maintain, and how much land and how many villages would be under their control, arranging for special army training.

**Campaigns against Ambadeva and the Yadavas/Pandyas:**

*   Prepared a three-phase strategy against Ambadeva and his allies, the Yadavas and Pandyas.
*   In **A.D. 1291**, sent a huge army against Tripuranthakam, Ambadeva's centre, under **Manumagannayya** (son of Kolani Somana mantri) and **Ayyadeva** (son of Induluri Pedda Gannayya mantri). The Kakatiya army won a great victory here — recorded in the Tripuranthakam inscription issued by Induluri Annayya (A.D. 1291) and supported by Parabrahma Sastry's account. No further inscription of Ambadeva is found at Tripuranthakam after A.D. 1291.
*   Ambadeva's son and successor **Murari II** ruled independently from Mulkinadu. Pratapa Rudra II sent a huge army under **Maharaya Patta Sahini Somaya** and **Induluri Annaya** against him; this war (before A.D. 1304) ended in a great Kakatiya victory, and the **Kayastha kingdom was merged into the Pratapa Rudra II's kingdom**, with **Soma Nayaka** appointed as administrator.

concepts.partName: Attacks of the Delhi Sultanate on Orugallu
concepts.bodyMd:
During Pratapa Rudra II's period, the Kakatiya kingdom — like the other contemporary kingdoms of the Yadavas, Hoyasalas, and Pandyas — faced attacks from the Delhi Sultanate.

*   In **A.D. 1295**, Delhi Sultan **Jalaluddin Khalji** sent a huge army under his son-in-law **Garshasp Malik (Garshans-i-Malik)** against Yadava Ramachandra's capital, **Devagiri**. The Yadava army was defeated; Ramachandradeva accepted Khalji overlordship, paid huge tribute in money and gold, and made peace. This defeat of the Yadavas endangered the standing of other Hindu kings in the region.
*   Pratapa Rudra II, in response, strengthened his army and defenses — building up infantry, war horses, elephants, and archers.

### First Muslim Attack on Telangana (A.D. 1303)

In **A.D. 1296**, **Garshasp Malik treacherously killed Jalaluddin Khalji**, his uncle and the Sultan of Delhi, and ascended the throne as **Allauddin Khalji**, ruling until A.D. 1316.

*   For the first time, Allauddin Khalji sent his army against **Trilinga/Telangana/Orugallu in A.D. 1303**. Delhi Sultanate army chiefs **Malik Fakruddin Jana and Zhujas of Kara** entered Telangana.
*   The historic battle took place at **Upperpalli village, Karimnagar district**; Kakatiya army chiefs **Potuganti Myli** and **Venna, son of Recherla Prasadaditya**, showed courage and talent, and repelled the Sultan's army — recorded in the Telugu writing _Velogotivari Vamshavali_.

### Second Attack on Orugallu by the Delhi Sultanate (A.D. 1309)

Allauddin Khalji, driven by ambition for a larger empire and by the sting of his earlier failure in Telangana, sent a huge army in **A.D. 1309** under the leadership of **Malik Kafur and Khwaja Haji**.

*   The Sultan's contingent entered Warangal via Devagiri, starting in **October 1309**.
*   In **February 1310**, a ferocious battle took place between the two sides; ultimately the Kakatiya emperor **accepted defeat and made a peace settlement**. Till Allauddin Khalji's death, Pratapa Rudra **paid tribute every year** and remained faithful to the Delhi Sultan.
*   Pratapa Rudra's feudatories rebelled against him because of this defeat and subordination: Nellore Telugu Choda king **Ranganatha** rebelled in the south, and Vaidumba chief **Mallideva**, based at Gandikota, also rebelled. Pratapa Rudra sent an army under **Juttayalenka Gonkayareddy** to suppress these rebels; after defeating Mallideva, Gonkayareddy was appointed the king's regent over Gandikota and nearby areas.
*   In **A.D. 1311**, the Delhi Sultan attacked the Pandya kingdom; Pratapa Rudra participated with his army at the Sultan's request. Sultan's chief **Malik Kafur** marched up to Madurai. Pratapa Rudra's chief **Muppidi Nayaka** played an important role in these campaigns.
*   In **A.D. 1316, Allauddin Khalji died**, and his army returned to Delhi. This allowed Pratapa Rudra's army to fight the Nellore ruler, **Ballala III of the Hoyasalas**, and the Pandya king **Veera Pandya**.
*   Pratapa Rudra's army chief defeated Hoyasala Ballala III and his ally, the Shambhuvaraya king of Padaiveedu, and the Chandragiri ruler Yadavaraya, in a fierce battle; Kanchi city was occupied — recorded in the Draksharamam temple inscription, preserved in the Mackenzie manuscripts. 

*   Kakatiya chiefs Muppidi Nayaka, Recherla Eradacha, and Manaveera and Deveri nayaka supported him in this campaign against the Pandya army; Sundara Pandya was placed on the Pandya throne as a result. 
*   As a mark of victory, Deveri nayaka made donations to the Ranganatha temple of Salakalaveedu village on the Kaveri Island.

*   Pratapa Rudra extended his dominion in the Dakshinapatha during **A.D. 1312–1316**.

### Pratapa Rudra II and the Politics of the Delhi Sultans (A.D. 1316–1317)

After Allauddin Khalji's death in A.D. 1316, his army chief **Malik Kafur** put the Sultan's son **Shahboddin** on the throne and continued administration — but was murdered soon after. **Taking this as an opportunity, Pratapa Rudra stopped paying yearly tribute.** Similarly, in the Yadava kingdom, Ramachandradeva's son-in-law **Harapaladeva** rebelled against the Sultan.

*   In this changed political scenario, Allauddin Khalji's other son **Qutubuddin Mubarak Shah** dethroned Shahboddin and ascended the Delhi throne. He sent an army against those Dakshinapatha kings who had earlier been his father's feudatories.
*   In **A.D. 1318**, he invaded Devagiri first, defeating and killing Harapala; Devagiri came under Delhi's control. Mubarak Shah then sent his army chief **Khusru Khan** against the Kakatiya kingdom. Historians such as Amir Khusru and Isami give differing accounts of this campaign; on the whole, a mutually agreed settlement was reached, and Pratapa Rudra accepted feudatory status under Mubarak Shah, paying tribute.

**War with Kampili (A.D. 1318):** Pratapa Rudra fought a war with Kampili ruler **Kumara Rama** in A.D. 1318. The main reason was that Kumara Rama had insulted Pratapa Rudra and disapproved of his helping Ballala III of the Hoyasala dynasty. \[Discrepancy between sources: the Kannada work _Kumara Ramana Charitra_ and the Telugu work _Bheemeshwara Puranam_ give different versions of the outcome — it seems that both sides may have claimed victory in this war.\]

### Ghiyasuddin Tughluq Ascends the Delhi Sultanate (A.D. 1320)

In A.D. 1318, Delhi court politics reached a peak of factionalism. Allauddin Khalji's son Qutubuddin ordered his army chief **Khusru Khan** to invade Mathura; Khusru Khan was ultimately murdered by the Turkey nobles, who then appointed **Ghiyasuddin Tughluq** as Delhi Sultan (A.D. 1320), starting the **Tughluq dynasty**.

*   Ghiyasuddin Tughluq's son **Ulug Khan** was sent to invade Warangal — first in **A.D. 1323**. Ulugh Khan failed in this first attempt, but on his father's orders made a second attack on Orugallu the same year.
*   Pratapa Rudra II and his army fought ferociously, but this time **Ulug Khan won**. The wealth and fort of Warangal became the target of the Sultanate army. While being taken captive to Delhi, **Pratapa Rudra escaped and committed suicide by jumping into the Narmada River** — recorded in the **Vilasa copper plate inscription of Masunuri Prolaya Nayaka**.
*   With Pratapa Rudra II's death, the **Kakatiya dynasty came to an end**. Telangana and Orugallu were merged into the Delhi Sultanate empire, and Orugallu's name was changed to **Sultanpur**.

**Pratapa Rudra II's feudatories, army chiefs, and ministers:** Kayastha Mallideva, Recherla Mummadi Nayaka, Recherla Venna (son of Recherla Prasadaditya), and his grandchildren Eradacha and Nalladacha were his key supporters.

concepts.partName: Delhi Sultanate Attacks on Dakshinapatha — Downfall of the Kakatiya Kingdom
concepts.bodyMd:
Under the Kakatiyas, today's Telangana and Andhra regions were united, and language and culture progressed. But the contemporary Deccan Hindu kingdoms — Hoyasala, Pandya, Yadava, and Kakatiya — all ended in the attacks of the Delhi Sultans, laying the foundation for the spread of Islam and Turkish political authority in the Dakshinapatha.

*   Muslim attacks on North India began around **A.D. 950**, whereas in South India they began only in **A.D. 1303**. The Slave dynasty ruled North India between A.D. 1206–1294; occupied with Mongol attacks and consolidating the north, and not cutting off relations with Afghanistan, the Delhi Sultans did not attempt southern conquests during this period. 

*   But by the time of the Khalji dynasty (beginning with Jalaluddin, continued by his son-in-law Allauddin Khalji), the Mongols were brought under control and the Rajputs were completely defeated.

*   Camped at Kara, Allauddin Khalji concluded that conquering the south was the way to meet the expenses of his army. By that time Devagiri was already occupied, so the "second step" fell invariably on Andhra. The south Indian kingdoms during the Muslim attacks had no strategy to work together or treat the threat as a common disaster — this lack of unity was a pathetic feature of the era's politics.

**Number of Turkish attacks:** Ekamranatha's Pratapa Charitra, Masunuri Prolaya Nayaka's Vilasa copper plate, the Anitally and Kaluvacheruvu copper plates, and other local histories record **eight Turkish attacks** during Pratapa Rudra II's period, though Muslim historians record only five.

1.  **A.D. 1303** — Malik Fakruddin Juna and Zaju attacked Telangana via Bengal for the first time; the two armies fought near Upperapalli in Karimnagar district, where Kakatiya chiefs Recherla Venna and Potuganti Myli led the Kakatiya army. **The Khalji army was defeated.**
2.  **A.D. 1309** — Second invasion, led by Malik Naib Kafur and Khwajahaji (described by contemporary historians Amir Khusru and Barani). The Khalji army reached Devagiri, then crossed Basirghar and Kunarbal to reach Anumakonda; after a month-long siege they occupied the mud fort, then attacked the stone fort, burning nearby villages. In this helpless situation, Pratapa Rudra II agreed to a treaty, paying a huge yearly tribute to Malik Kafur.
3.  **Third attack** — After Allauddin Khalji's death, Pratapa Rudra stopped paying tribute; Qutubuddin Mubarak (the Delhi Sultan at that time) sent Khusru Khan against Orugallu. Pratapa Rudra was defeated and again accepted to pay tribute via a peace treaty.
4.  **A.D. 1321–22 — Fourth attack**
    *   In 1320 Khalji rule ended at Delhi and Tughluq rule began; Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, wanting to build a Muslim rule in the south instead of merely collecting tribute, sent his son **Juna Khan**, who reached Orugallu via Devagiri and attacked for six months.
    *   When the Tughluq army was about to win, poet **Ubaid spread a rumour of the Delhi Sultan's death**, and two army chiefs, **Taimur and Tigrin, rebelled** and began discussions with Pratapa Rudra; Juna Khan stopped the attack and returned to Delhi, and while retreating, the Kakatiya army caused them great loss and trouble.
5.  **A.D. 1323 — Fifth attack**
    *   Juna Khan reached Devagiri, and with additional reinforcements from Delhi occupied Bidar and Bodhan, then attacked Orugallu; the siege continued for five months, emptying Pratapa Rudra's treasury and creating fear and panic among the people through the wanton destruction of villages.
    *   **Jealousy between the Velamas and Reddys reached its peak** — Pratapa Rudra's respect for the Velamas was resented by the Reddys, and army chief **Bobba Reddy left the war with his army**; the protection of the Kakatiya kingdom was fractured by these **caste differences**, and **Pratapa Rudra was defeated by Juna Khan and taken captive**. While being taken to Delhi, he escaped and committed suicide by jumping into the Narmada River. The Kakatiya kingdom became part of the Delhi Sultanate; Orugallu, popularly known as "Andhra nagari," was changed to **Sultanpur**.

The Kakatiyas ruled from **A.D. 1163 to 1323**, with Orugallu as their capital city. Historians hold differing opinions on the exact form and nature of their administration; the Kakatiyas broadly followed the traditional system of administration already existing in India and South India — as in all Hindu kingdoms, the son held the hereditary right to succeed the throne. Though of **Sudra** origin, the Kakatiyas followed ancient Raja Dharma and Raja Neeti as laid down by the ancient law-writers.

*   Since Ganapatideva had no sons, he trained his daughter Rudramadevi in political administration and declared her his successor, thus **starting a new tradition**.
*   The **Manadala system** was a new system introduced by the Kakatiyas in the central government; they encouraged powerful **Mandalikas** and cultivated friendship with them.
*   Rudramadevi declared her grandson Pratapa Rudra as her successor, and he ascended the throne after her.

**Nature of the administration — historian debate:**

*   One opinion holds that the Kakatiyas followed a **hereditary despotic political system**.
*   According to **P.V. Parabrahma Sastry**, their administration was built on **decentralization of power** — proven by the strengthening of feudatories/the feudal system, though there are differing opinions on whether this feudatory system strengthened or weakened Kakatiya administration.
*   Historian **C.V. Ramachandra Rao** held that Kakatiya administration was very close to a **"segmentary state"**, as proposed by American historian Burton Stein.
*   Among all these opinions, the **most widely accepted** view is that the Kakatiya administration was a **decentralized system**.

**Administrative lineage:** The decentralized, seventy-two Niyoga administrative system is understood to follow the pattern of the Western Chalukya administration. The Kakatiya **Nayankara system** is considered, per Parabrahma Sastry, the **precursor to the Vijayanagara period's Amara Nayaka system**. Administration moved step by step from village, to district, to state, to central government, with powers clearly defined at each level, though feudatories also played an important role alongside these formal levels.

**Titles and governance style:** Though the emperor held all power, the Kakatiya rulers did not adopt grand titles like "Maharajadhiraja" or "Parameshwara" — instead they used simple titles similar to their own feudatories, such as "Samadigata Panch mahasabda" and "Mahamandaleshwara." They did not rule as autocrats regarding themselves as sovereign monarchs. The Kakatiyas introduced a new type of administration in which they dominated the internal administration of their feudatories while ensuring feudatory power never grew too strong, and made appointments of administrative officials throughout the empire.

*   During the Kakatiya period, feudatories rebelled only once — the **A.D. 1290 rebellion of Kayastha Ambadeva** — because feudatories were generally treated as **co-rulers**. The Kakatiyas respected local traditions and continued them in conquered regions; for example, they took no action against their feudatory Cheruku family, who never even mentioned the Kakatiyas as their sovereigns.

**Council of Ministers:** Inscriptions and literature show that the king administered through a council of ministers. The Kakatiyas followed the concept that the state consists of **seven limbs (saptanga samanvita)**. 

Contemporary works like _Neetisaram_, _Neeti sastra muktavalli_, and _Pratapa Rudra Yashobhushanam_ discuss the duties and role of the king in political affairs, his authority over ministers, officials, and forts, and matters of safety. The council consisted of ministers, Amatyas, Preggadas, feudatories, and Dandanayakas, though their precise portfolios and authorities are not clearly known.

*   **Malyala Hemadri reddy** was the **Mahapradhani** during Ganapatideva's period, while **Muppidi Nayaka** held this position under Pratapa Rudra.
*   The contemporary work "Purushartha saram," written by Siva Devayya during Ganapatideva's reign, records that the king met daily with all his ministers to discuss administrative matters.
*   All administrative affairs (civil and military) were divided into **72 Niyogas (classes)**; the official who controlled all these Niyogas was the **Niyogadhipati**. During Ganapatideva's period, Kayastha **Gangayya sahini** held this post; during Rudramamba's period, **Tripuri and Ponka Malllaya Pragada** acted as Bahattar Niyogadhipati.

### Regional Administration

The Kakatiyas divided their empire into **Rastra, Sthala, Seema, Nadu Bhumi, and Garma** for administrative convenience — names found in inscriptions of Ganapatideva's and Pratapa Rudra's periods. The Srisailam inscription (of Pratapa Rudra II) mentions divisions such as Naravadi nadu, Motavadi, Pakanadu, Renadu, Mulikinadu, Are Bhumi, Kandurunadu, Venginadu, Velanadu, Natavadi, Eruvanadu, Sakalinadu, and Prolinadu.

*   A **Sthalam** is an area comprising **twenty-four villages**; Sthalams were numerous in number. In the Warangal inscription, Anumkonda, Mattewada, and Orugallu together form one Sthalam.
*   What control the central government exercised over the officials of the Rastra is not clearly known from any source.

### Village Administration

During the Kakatiya period, the village remained the lowest level of administration, as in earlier periods. The village's officers, collectively, were known as **Ayyagars** — an already-established system before the Kakatiyas, with **twelve** officers.

Named village officials found in inscriptions include: **Karanam, Reddy, Talari, Purohita, Kammari, Kamsali, Vadrangi, Kummari, Chakali, Mangali, Vetti, Charmakara, and Niruduvadu.** All were given tax-free land for performing their services, and among them, **Karanam, Reddy, and Talari** were the government officials, who also received a share of the crop.

### Army Administration

The Kakatiyas maintained a large, well-trained army — their many victories against the Yadavas, Hoyasalas, Pandyas, and Muslim invaders support this. Contemporary political works (Baddena's _Neetishastra muktavalli_, Madiki Singhana's _Sakala Neeti Sammatam_) also help in understanding army administration during this period, though these cannot be treated as complete or unbiased, since the authors held important administrative positions themselves.

**Forts:** The Kakatiyas gave importance to protecting the empire through forts; political thinkers of the period considered a ruler with strongly fortified defenses very difficult to defeat. As mentioned in the _Neetisaram_ of Pratapa Rudra, there were **four types of forts**: **Sthala** (land), **Jala** (water), **Vana** (forest), and **Giri** (hill). 

*   Forts built by the Kakatiyas — **Orugallu, Raichuru, Golakonda, Bhuvanagiri, Rachakonda, Devarakonda, Nalgonda, and Panugallu** — were considered invincible.

**Nayankara system:** The administrative/military system distributed lands to military officials called **Nayakas**. A village or villages given to a Nayaka is known as **Nayakasthala** or Nayakasthala vritti; there was no clear, fixed definition of the Nayakas' characteristics or responsibilities, and the _Neetisaram_ of Pratapa Rudra offers only limited guidance here.

*   To maintain the fourfold army (**Chaturanga balas**) and fill the treasury, the king was to keep the larger, higher-income villages for himself and give smaller villages to subordinates, per Pratapa Rudra's own guidance. 

*   Here "Nayakas" effectively means "subordinates." Villages given to Nayakas were of two types: small villages given for their maintenance (no separate salary paid), and income from bigger villages, part of which was paid to the king as tribute while the rest was spent maintaining troops for the king's service. 

**Forces:** Kakatiya kings maintained, with discipline, **Ashwa (horse), Gaja (elephant), Ratha (charioteers), and Kalbala (foot soldiers)** forces — mentioned in contemporary works. 

The army of Pratapa Rudradeva consisted of **100 elephants, 20,000 horses, and nine lakh foot soldiers**. Officials in charge were known as **Gaja sahini and Ashwa sahini**. The Nalgonda inscription of Ganapatideva records that Kayastha **Gangaya sahini** was brought from North India to maintain the horse force. **Induluri Annaya** led the five lakh foot soldiers; **Jayapa senani** was Gaja sahini during Ganapatideva's period, while **Bendapudi Annayya** was Gajabaladhyaksha during Pratapa Rudra's period.

*   The army had two types of military organisation: the **Moolabalam (main force)** or **Sthirabalam (standing army)**, under the direct control of the king or his appointed officials (such as Gaja sahini and Ashwa sahini), and a **subordinate army**.
*   Along with army strength, the Kakatiyas gave importance to forts (Vana, Giri, Sthala, and Jala forts existed); _Neetisaram_ and _Prushartha saram_ both explain the importance of fort protection. The Kakatiya armies' fierce, heroic resistance against the Delhi Sultan's forces stands as ample proof of their military strength and valour.

### Judicial System

The Kakatiya rulers followed the judicial code that had existed in South India for ages; several inscriptions record different types of legal disputes.

**Example 1 — Village boundary dispute (A.D. 1214, Duggirala, Guntur district):** After conquering Velanadu, while camping in the region, Ganapatideva was approached by the people of Poondi, Mormapoondi, and Eevani villages to resolve a boundary dispute. 

*   He asked his ministers **Mallavaraju and Rudraraju** to solve it; they heard arguments from the people of all three villages and consulted the opinion of the **Mahajanas**. **Sooravaraju of Eevani village** (likely its Karanam) was chosen for his clear understanding of the boundaries, and the dispute was resolved using his experience.
*   This inscription shows that **Mahajanas and Karanams** were recognized as judicious persons; such a judicial meeting held outside the capital, in a village, in the presence of ministers, is termed an "**Aprathisthista sabha.**"

**Example 2 — Water canal dispute (A.D. 1246, Karimnagar):** A dispute arose between two villages over rights to a village tank's water canal in "Nedhapur" village. Local officials Ravidattu, Nathadeva, and Hingadeva explained the dispute to Ganapatideva, who assigned the matter to **Manchiraju**, minister of Jayapa senani. 

*   Manchiraju visited the village, discussed the matter with the Mahajanas and elders of Chamanapally, Kummarikunta, Devanapally, and Katlakolapally, and submitted a report to Ganapatideva. 
*   The king discussed the matter with the local representative **Akshayadeva** and finally ordered his judgment communicated to the people and local officials — though the people were initially unhappy, they accepted Akshayadeva's judgment. 
*   Ganapatideva then had the judgment engraved on copper plates and executed: the Mahajanas of Chamanapally were granted overall rights over the canal, and other villages had no rights over its water.

These two judgments — termed a "**Shashita Aprathisthita Sabha**" — reveal how righteous Kakatiya-period judgments were; the opinion of villagers was given significant importance in delivering judgments.

The Kakatiyas belong to the early medieval period, during which religion had considerable influence on society — the relations and associations of different classes of people, their place in society, and the social distance among various classes were all shaped by religious change and upheaval. 

Along with the four Varnas, many castes and sub-castes emerged during this period, formed on the basis of occupation; hereditary occupations became castes, each with its own rules and restrictions, regulated by caste associations known as **"Kula Samayas."** These Kula Samayas had tremendous influence on the life of their members. Friction between the Saiva, Vaishnava, and Jaina religious sects created disunity in society and obstructed the unity of various groups.

### Caste System

The Kakatiyas, after achieving political power, declared themselves **Kshetriyas**. While the Cholas and Chalukyas also declared themselves Kshetriyas, many ruling families in the Andhra region instead proudly declared themselves belonging to the **"fourth caste" (Chaturtha kulajas)**, without claiming Kshetriya lineage.

*   The Kakatiyas, too, did not come forward to claim Kshetriya status until Ganapatideva's period. After Ganapatideva became a great conqueror, uniting the whole of Andhradesa politically as emperor, he declared himself **Kshetrya** — though historians and sociologists note there is no true Kshetriya caste in South India.
*   The Kakatiyas did not clearly state their caste in their own inscriptions; Ganapatideva's inscriptions mention them as **Suryavamsha (Solar) Kshetriyas**, while Vidyanatha wrote that Pratapa Rudra's dynasty excelled that of both Surya (Solar) and Chandra (Lunar) vamsha Kshetriyas.

**Religious/caste conflicts:** Kakatiya-period society was in a transition phase, marked by severe religious conflicts, class wars, and socio-religious jealousy.

*   As per Pratapa Rudra Charitra, when Pratapa Rudra donated golden cows to learned Brahmins, some Brahmins who did not receive cows instigated some **Chandalas** to agitate for the dead cows. Similarly, the Visva Brahmins, Saiva Brahmins, and Vaidiki Brahmins fought among themselves before the king, each claiming sole authority over astrology, trying to prove their own superiority.
*   **Poetess Molla**, who belonged to the fourth caste, wrote a Ramayana and tried to dedicate her work to King Pratapa Rudra — this was obstructed by Brahmins, who came forward to have the _Bhaskara Ramayana_ read instead of the _Molla Ramayanam_. In this helpless situation, Pratapa Rudra simply honoured Molla without formally accepting the dedication of her work.
*   In this period Bhakti movement reached an extreme state: **Chakrapani Ranganatha**, a Vaishnava preacher, got himself blinded to avoid seeing the Tripuranthakam (Saiva) temple gopuram. **Veera Saiva preacher Palkuriki Somanatha** abused the Vaidiki Brahmins as "karma chandalas," "vrata bhrastas," and "pashukaras," and called Vaishnavas "Namala Kukkalu" (dogs of Namas); he held that Jaina and Buddhism should be destroyed. **Pratapa Charitram** and **Siddheshwara Charitram** record clashes between Veerasaiva scholars and Jaina/Buddhist scholars.
*   Against this backdrop of intolerance, some figures — like **Swamy Dandanayaka and Bekkallu Mallireddy**, who called themselves **"Chatussamaya summuddaranalu"** — showed extreme tolerance. Against the extreme Saiva-Vaishnava rivalry, **Poet Tikkana Somayaji** preached **Harihara tatvamu** (the combined philosophy of Vishnu and Shiva).

This religious intolerance obstructed social unity and influenced socio-political systems of the time. Kakatiya rulers, however, appointed people of all castes to government service; in both the Moolabalam (main army) and Nayankara (subordinate) army, importance was given to all communities as much as possible.

*   Pratapa Rudra had given more importance to the **Velamas**, which upset the Reddys; to make Pratapa Rudra realize this, in one of the wars, **Terala Bhoj Reddy** and his followers **left the war** — their aim was to make him recognize their importance in protecting the king and kingdom, but the plan backfired: they lost both the king and the kingdom. 

*   This lack of unity and the resulting unrest contributed to the **downfall of the Kakatiya kingdom**; this social unrest due to caste conflicts led to the establishment of the **Bahamani kingdom** after the Kakatiya downfall.

**Caste associations ("Samayas"):** A unique feature of Kakatiya-period society was caste associations called **"Samayas."** The Brahmin Samaya was known as **"Mahajanas"** and the Vaishya Samayas as **"Nakara."** "Sanimunnuru," "Telikivepuru," and "Panchanam" were some other samayas. 

*   Inscriptions mention 'Uru' (village) samayas and 'Sthala' (local) samayas at different levels; these Samayas held special powers — safeguarding and collecting taxes, resolving disputes, etc., for the people of that caste. 
*   10th–11th century inscriptions mention **Ashtadash (eighteen) samayas** in society. 
*   Among Brahmins, the **Vaidiki (ritualistic)** section was also seen in government service.

**Social trends:** During this period, the political importance of Brahmins declined while the prominence of the fourth caste increased; the fourth caste enhanced its social respect and hierarchy, and the ruling class made matrimonial alliances with influential people from it. The caste system was not strong or rigid. 

*   Negative social habits also increased across all castes: **child marriages, Varasulka (bride-price), forced widowhood, and Sati sahagamanam** were seen frequently. 
*   Common people remained largely far from education. **Drinking, gambling, cockfights, and bull fights** were common.

In the early days of Kakatiya rule in the Deccan plateau, they had scanty water resources and less fertile land in the Telangana region. Ganapatideva, through his military victories, brought the fertile coastal Andhra region under Kakatiya authority. 

Through agricultural taxes and taxes on trade and commerce, considerable income reached the treasury. Contemporary historians and travellers — **Barani, Isami, Ferishtha, and Marco Polo** — mentioned the Kakatiyas' wealth and richness in their writings. 

Kakatiya rulers and their feudatories showed special interest in agricultural development, constructing tanks and canals, and in some places clearing forests to convert them into agricultural land. Along with agriculture, internal and external trade, and industries developed. There are no surviving sources giving exact figures for Kakatiya income and expenditure.

### Agriculture

Agricultural land was divided into two types: **Magani (wet land)** and **Metta (dry land)**.

*   Within Magani: **Neeru nela (water land)** and **Thota (garden land)**.
*   In Metta (dry) land, rain-dependent crops such as **Maize, Mustard seeds, Castor seeds, and Sessamam** were grown.
*   Irrigated lands were known as **"Acchu Kattu"** lands, and the government treasury collected land tax on these lands. When land was leased, the agreement between owner and lessee was formalized by the exchange of **Tambulam (betel leaves)**.

Villages were numerous during the Kakatiya period, and the majority of people's occupation was agriculture. Inscriptions record that the Kakatiyas and their feudatories built many new villages — **Manthena, Chennuru, Kaleshwaram, Narasampeta, Achampeta, Khammammetta, and Kothagudem**, among others.

*   Kakatiya rulers and feudatories also built new tanks. For example, during Ganapatideva's period, his feudatory **Prolaraju**, ruling over Chennuru rajya, built a new village and a tank, collecting for it **one-sixteenth of a ruka per marutur land** (one visa as the god's portion) — recorded in the A.D. 1303 **Katakuru inscription** of Pratapa Rudra.
*   Important agricultural crops of the period: **paddy, cotton, ulavalu (horsegram), oilseeds, millets (jonnalu), vegetables, chilies, black gram, green gram, ginger, sugarcane, wheat, onions, and blue (neeli) dye**. Flowers and fruits were grown in special gardens.

**Taxes on agriculture:** Named taxes found in inscriptions include **Siddayam, Oir Pangamu, Pannu, Kanika, Darishanamu, Vennu Pannu, Neeruveedi, Ardhayam, and Pullari (tax on grassland)**. Tax was collected either in cash or kind; **tax was exempted** on lands given to Brahmins, temples, and village servants.

*   The **Manthena inscription** records that Brahmin Manchibhattu, a Rajapurohita, donated a wide tract of land with the king's permission.
*   Ganapatideva's **Kaleshwaram inscription** records that Lord Budhadeva, son of Rudra, donated four nivartanas of land near the village tank.
*   Many villages were named after the Kakatiya kings and queens who built them: **Ganapavaram** (by Ganapatideva), **Mahadevapuram** (by Mahadeva), **Rudravaram** (by Rudra), **Bayyaram** (by Bayyaladevi), and **Muppavaram** (by Muppamamba).

**Land ownership debate:** The **A.D. 1311 inscription from Mellacheruvu (Nalgonda district)** records that the king held all rights over **Rachapolamu** (regadi or veligadu/sandy soil) lands, and could distribute these lands to Brahmins or farmers as he wished.

*   Building villages and excavating tanks was considered a **meritorious deed (Poonya)** in Kakatiya-period society. Ganapatideva's sister **Kundamamba** built "Kundavaram" village in the Chennuru taluqa of Adilabad district and excavated a tank called "Kunda Samudram" after herself. Ganapatideva's teacher (Guru), **Visweshvara Sivacharya**, purchased forest land for 850 gadyanas, cleared it, built a village named "Visvanathapura" after himself, and excavated a tank there.
*   The king gave special tax exemptions on land around newly built villages to encourage cultivation. Nayankara ministers, army chiefs, Karanams, village servants, and Ayyagars were given tax-free land in the villages where they lived.
*   Ganapatideva's daughter **Ganapamba's Mogalutla inscription** records that village servants such as **Kammarlu (blacksmiths), Kummarlu (potters), and Chakali (washermen)** had to donate half the income from their cultivated land to the donee. **Rachapolam/Racha bhumulu** (king's lands) are mentioned in the Mellacheruvu inscription. Newly cultivated land was known as **"Podu,"** and inscriptional evidence shows tax exemptions were granted for such newly cultivated lands.

### Irrigation System

The Kakatiyas took special care to provide water to agricultural lands, and tank excavation proceeded briskly during their rule. Big tanks were called **"samudram"** and were constructed as a chain system — when upper tanks filled, extra water flowed into lower-level tanks, a system called **"Golusukattu cheruvulu"** (tanks constructed in a chain system). Motupalli and Bayyaram inscriptions give details of the period's tanks.

Along with tanks, water springs and canals played an important role in irrigation — inscriptions mention 'Gosugu canal,' 'Ravipati canal,' Moosati canal, Aleti canal, Kuchineni canal, and Bommakanti canal. Water was also drawn from wells using **Etams and pulleys**; the A.D. 1254 Dosapadu inscription records donations of bulls and wood for making pulleys/etams.

*   Tanks and canals were **repaired every year**; persons appointed to maintain them were paid **one kuncha of grain for every putti of grain** produced under these canals — a system called **"Dashbandha" or "Dashavandha manyam."** Some land was also given as manyam to those carrying out this maintenance work.
*   This level of irrigation care was not continued after the Kakatiyas. Farmers of the period worshipped bulls, ploughs, and agricultural implements before beginning agricultural activities, celebrating them as festivals — **'Eruvaka' and Sankranti** remain major farmers' festivals even today.

### Village Economy

The Kakatiyas ruled for over two and a half centuries with Anumakonda and Warangal as capitals; the village remained the base of administration and economy. Agricultural land was divided into 'Magani' (wetland, sub-divided into **Neerunela** — crop-growing land — and **Tontanela** — garden land) and 'Metta' (dryland, growing sesamam, castor seeds, blue dye/neelimandu, and ragulu). Lands tilled with ploughs were called **'Achukattu nela'** — "Achukattu" referring to a tax called 'Ari' collected on such lands.

Many varieties of paddy were grown; in the **Orugallu region**, a scented paddy variety was cultivated. Coconut, guava, mango, banana, and betel-leaf gardens were common. Jaggery, sugar, and oil-pressing industries were found in nearly every village. The number of cows donated to temples, per inscriptional data, indicates the cattle wealth of the period.

### Industries – Inland and Foreign Trade

Along with agriculture, many industries developed. Palkuriki Somanatha, in his Basavapuranam, mentions **20 varieties of cloth**. Marco Polo wrote that high-quality cloth appreciated even by kings was woven in **Mysolia (Machilipatanam)**. In Warangal, **Ratnakamballu (quality woollen blankets)** and **Makhmal (fine cloth)** were woven.

*   Many handicrafts made of different metal alloys (**pancha lohas**) were produced; inscriptions mention metal lamps, bronze hand lamps, plates, and hand bells. The **Palanati Veera Charitra** records that Brahmanaidu erected a panch loha flag post (pillar) at the Tripuranthakam temple.
*   **Guttikonda and Palanatiseema** were famous for iron industries; weapons used in wars were locally manufactured. **Swords made at Nirmal (Adilabad district)** became popular even in foreign countries. Marco Polo also mentioned diamond mines in the **Golconda** region (diamond mines existed in Rayalaseema too). Carpenters made colourful **Ratnas (water pulleys)** and ivory boxes; **wax dolls (Lakka Bommalu)** and other sport items were made in Andhra Pradesh. Coloring of puppets used in puppet shows became a major industry.
*   Important commercial centres of the period included **Orugallu, Panagallu, Jedcherla, Alampur, Maktal, Manthena, Peruru, Velpuru, Tripuranthakam, Penugonda, Kocherlakota, Pedaganjam, Nelluru, Ghantasala, Gudivada, Durgi, Macherla, Tangeda, Enamadala, Lebaka, Nandaluru, Upperapalle, Mopuru, and Dornala.** 

*   The Warangal fort inscription of Ganapatideva records the various businesses conducted by traders in market yards; these traders were organized into **Shrenis (guilds)**.

**Trade guilds:** Shrenis/guilds, which flourished in Andhra during the Satavahana period (both occupational/craft guilds and trade guilds), continued to play an important role in Kakatiya-period trade and commerce. 

The A.D. 1282 Tripuranthakam inscription records that "**Nanadesi Pekkandru**," a trading guild, received permission for trading from the king. Both occupational and trading guilds carried on business jointly. Each guild elected a head, called **'Shresthi' or Setti**, and members' problems were solved within the guild itself; each guild had its own official insignia and maintained its own army for protection. The businessman was called **'Behari'** and the business itself **'Vyavaharam.'**

*   Two types of trade were carried out by guilds: **Swadeshi (inland)** — called "Nakaram" — and **Paradeshi (foreign)** — called "Nanadeshi Pekkandru" / "Ubhaya nanadeshi pekkandru." 

*   The **Aiyyavole-500 guild** did not have a good reputation in the Telugu area during the Kakatiya period. Guilds donated a share of their profits to temples/gods. 
*   **Vaisyas** were superior in business; some inscriptions link Vaisya guilds with Reddy, Naidu, Boya, and Dasari communities.

*   The **Veerabananja Samaya (shreni)** received permission to trade in Pakanadu, Vengi, and Anumakonda cities.
*   Guild names found in inscriptions: **Swadesi, Paradesi, Vaadalavaru, Saasar booru, Tagarambur, Ubhaya Nanadessi**, etc. Trade and commerce were centred on the Vaisya community, known as **Chettis, Settis, or Shresttis**. Baddena's Neetisastramuktavalli likens the importance of the Vaisya community to a city as breath is to life, water to a crop, and a trunk to an elephant. Kings encouraged Vaisyas in their trade and commerce.
*   The A.D. 1268 Mahaboobabad inscription of Rudramadevi mentions one **Preggada Daram Govindasetti**; the Draksharamam inscription of Kulothunga Gonkaraja's mentions **Setti Surapa setti**; another inscription mentions **Ayyapareddy, son of Reddy Sunkana** — suggesting Reddys were also appointed as **"Raja Settis."** Trade could not be conducted without the king's permission.

**Commercial routes and foreign trade:** With the growth of inland trade, foreign trade also prospered. Commercial centres were well connected to ports by highways — for example, Motupalli, Machilipatanam, Andhra, and Karnataka were well connected by highways from Motupalli to Bellary via Tripuranthakam. A trade route from Palanadu connecting Nalagonda, via Nakarekall, to Orugallu is mentioned in the _Kridhabhirammam_.

*   Based on inscriptional references to taxes levied on ports, it is understood that the **Krishna and Godavari rivers** were used as waterways. **Motupalli was the centre of foreign trade**; other important foreign trade ports included **Krishnapatanam, Hamsaladeevi, and Machilipatanam**.
*   Ganapatideva issued the **"Abhaya sasana"** at Motupalli, giving assurances to foreign traders. The Motupalli inscription details imports and exports from the port: elephants, horses, gold, jewels, sandalwood, camphor, camphor oil, rose water, ivory, copper, tin, lead, mercury, silk, ruby, and other "Sughandha dravvalu" (fragrant goods). **Trade was conducted with China, Persia, Arabia, Ceylon, and the East India islands.**
*   The rate of tax was fixed based on the quality of goods — for example, if 30 elephants were traded, one elephant had to be paid as tax. Ganapatideva assured that **taxes would be lesser** for traders, and that government officials would not exploit traders, ensuring trade was carried out ethically without cheating people.
