Prior to the rise of Kakatiya power in Telangana, the people had shown some inclination toward **Jainism and Buddhism**.

### Jainism

During the Western Chalukya period, Jainism enjoyed special patronage among the people of Telangana. **Nizamabad (Bodhan), Karimnagar (Vemulawada), Medak (Kolcharam, Patancheruvu), Nalgonda (Kollipaka/Kolanupaka), and Warangal (Anumakonda)** were important Jaina centres. 

Kakatiya rulers of the first generation followed and patronized Jainism, even though the Eastern Chalukyas were patrons of Vedic religion. The _Orugallu Kaifiyat_ records that Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra indulged in violence against a Jain ascetic, Rushbhanatha, who then went to Anumakonda and got shelter there. **Prolaraja's Anumakonda inscription begins with a prayer to Jinendra.** 

Slowly, Jainism and Buddhism lost the patronage of the local people and kings, and Saivism and Vaishnavism became prominent instead.

*   The **Vemulawada Chalukyas** patronized Jainism; their court poet, the Jaina scholar **Somadevasuri**, wrote "Yashastilaka," and poet **Pampa** wrote "Adipuranam." The **Sanigaram inscription** records a donation made to Yudhamalla Jinalaya by Betaraju I. **Betaraju II** made donations to Jaalna Jaina basadi.
*   **Prolaraju's A.D. 1117 Padmakshi temple inscription** (Warangal) records that his wife **Mailamma** made donations for the construction of the Kadalaraya Jaina basadi.
*   Jaina poet **Appayyarya** wrote _Jinendra Kalyanabhyudayam_ during Pratapa Rudradeva's period.

**Jaina sculpture earlier than the Kakatiya period:** Before the expansion of Kakatiya power, Jainism was popular in Telangana during the Rashtrakuta and Chalukya periods, and many Jaina basadis were built. **Chilkuru, Kulcharam (Medak), Patancheruvu, Kolanupaka, Hanumakonda, and Polavasa** had sculptures of Jaina Thirthankaras. 

The **Parshvanatha sculpture found at Kulcharam** (Medak district) is particularly notable — nine feet tall, seated under a seven-headed Nagaraju (serpent) canopy, with a serenely-faced idol carved delicately, hands reaching to the knees. 

The inscription at its base reads "Sri Chalukya kula tilakam Tailavarasan," dating it to the period of **Tailapa II (A.D. 973–995)**. The sculptures found at Chilkuru and Patancheruvu are in a dilapidated state and preserved in the State Archaeology Museum, Hyderabad.

### Saivism

Saivism received the fullest patronage of the Kakatiyas. During their period, **Kalamukha, Pashupata, Aradhya, and Veerasaiva** were the sub-sects of Saivism practiced. Early Kakatiyas followed and patronized the **Kalamukha** sect specifically.

*   The Anumakonda inscription records that **Betaraju II** was a disciple of **Rameshwara pandita**, head of Seelamatham in Srisailam — a great scholar of "Lakuleshwara Agama Mahasiddhantam" (Lakuleshwara/Sakuleshwara being the founder of Kalamukha philosophy). Rameshwara pandita gave Siva diksha to Betaraju's sons Durgaraju and Prolaraju II. 

*   The Kalamukha saivas of Karnataka regarded **Srisailam** as their centre and Rameshwara Pandita as their teacher (guru), underlining Srisailam's importance. Rameshwara Pandita was also Sthanapati of the Draksharamam temple; the Kakatiya kings maintained friendly relations with Kalamukha teachers.

*   **Alampur** (on the banks of the Tungabhadra, present Mahaboobnagar district) was a famous Saiva kshetra; its Sthanapatis at the Brahmeshwara temple were pious scholars. **Agastheshwaram** near Alampur was another Kalamukha centre; notable Sthanapatis of the Brahmeshwara Matham included Lokabharanam pandita, Someshwara bhattaraka, Brahmarishi bhattaraka, and Dharindrasi pandita.
*   **Vemulawada** (Karimnagar district) was once a great Saiva kshetra patronized by Kalyana Chalukya kings — Tailapa II donated to Maheshvara Shakti pandita of the Kalamukha matham, and Mahamandaleshvara Rajaditya donated to the presiding deity of the Rajarajeshwara Swamy matham.
*   **Prolaraja II's teacher, Rameshwara pandita, settled at Kaleshwaram** (Warangal district) and consecrated the Siva linga there.

*   Important Kalamukha Saiva kshetras in Kakatiya-period Telangana included **Dharmapuri (Karimnagar), Anumakonda (Warangal), Ainavolu (Warangal), Panagallu (Nalgonda), Nizamabad, Nandikandi (Medak), and Sanigaram (Karimnagar)**. 
*   In Rayalaseema, **Pushpagiri** near Kadapa was a great Kalamukha kshetra; in the coastal region, **Amaravati, Samarlkota, Bheemavaram, Palkollu, and Draksharama Bheemeshwara temple** were the great Kalamukha kshetras (per M. Krishnakumari's _Pancharamas in Medieval Andhradesa_, 1989).

**Pashupatas / Saiva sidhantas — second important sect:** Agamas were the main sources for this sect, which followed the "Yoganisthas" and remained attached to Siva temples. **Mattamayura**, a branch of the Golakhi matha, organized itself and sought royal patronage alongside the Vedic Brahmins. 

The Kalachuri kingdom, spreading around Jabalpur (Madhya Pradesh), became the prominent centre of Saiva sidhanta; **Rannad and Kadvaha mathas** were the early Saiva mathas there. Kalachuri kings Yashakarma, Gajagarna, Narasimha, Jayasimha, and Vijayasimha had close relations with Pashupata Siva yogis; **Sadasivayogi, Purandhara yogi, and Prabhasiva yogi** acted as teachers to Kalachuri kings.

*   In the **13th century**, when political disturbance and instability struck the Kalachuri kingdom, its Saiva teachers migrated to Andhradesa. **Dharmasiva** came to Draksharama before A.D. 1234 and settled there, becoming the teacher of **Ganapatideva**. 
*   During Ganapatideva's time, at temples under Kakatiya control — Tripuranthakam, Bhattiprolu, Eleshwaram (Nalgonda), Manthena, Mandadam, Kaleshwaram (Karimnagar), Malkapuram (Guntur), Somasila (Mahaboobnagar), Visveshwara — Sivadeshika **established Saiva Golaki mathas** and was elevated to the position of **Rajaguru** — Rajaguru to both Ganapatideva and his daughter Rudramadevi.
*   Per Rudramadevi's **Malkapuram inscription (A.D. 1261)**, on the wish of her father Rudramadevi donated Mandam village on the banks of the Krishna in Velanati vishaya to **Visveshvara shambu**, who constructed a Sudha Saiva matham, food-feeding house, and Sivalaya there — this became popular as the **Golaki matham**.

*   The Mandama village settlement had three teachers for Vedas, five for Logic/Literature, and Agamas, with free boarding and lodging provided to students (recorded across multiple inscriptions in _Medieval Andhra Desh Religious Institutions_, translated by G. Anjaia). 
*   This Golaki matham also had a **hospital with a delivery room**.

*   **Visveshvara shambhu** also established a Sivalaya and Upala matha on the banks of the Godavari at Kaleshwaram. Branches of the Golaki mathas were established at Pushpagiri, Sriparvatam, Tripuranthakam, Alampur, Draksharamam, Bhattiprolu, etc. — all headed by Sivacharyas. 

*   The Golaki mathas enjoyed prominence up to Pratapa Rudra's period before declining. **Srisailam** had an **Abhinava Golaki matham** in this period, maintained partly through donations by Kayastha Jannigadeva.

*   **Umamaheshvaram, Alampur, Tripuranthakam, and Pushpagiri** (Srisailam's entry kshetras) received strong royal and popular patronage. Temple priests called **Maheshvarlu** became very powerful.

**Religious tolerance:** The Kakatiyas' policy of religious tolerance helped sow tolerance among all religious sects of the period. In contemporary Karnataka, conflicts between Veerasaiva and Saiva sects were common — this was not seen in Andhra desa, owing to the Kakatiyas' tolerant policy. Kakatiya rulers and their royal teachers preached religious harmony and peaceful living, seen by later generations as an ideal model.

### Vaishnavism

Kakatiya rulers gave their people complete religious freedom. The **Varaha insignia** (boar symbol) on their signs and coins, and Vaishnava idols erected in temples they built, show their religious tolerance.

*   **Rudradeva** built the **Trikuta (Rudreshwara) temple** at Anumakonda, erecting the idol of Vasudeva there. His minister **Vellanki Gangadhara** erected the Prasanna Keshava swamy idol and built a large temple at Anumakonda.
*   **Ganapatideva's sister, Rani Mylamba**, built the temple for Gopalakrishna at **Inugurti** and made several donations for its maintenance.
*   **Pratapa Rudra II's** army general **Devari Nayaka**, on his king's orders, donated Sakalveedu village to the Ranganatha Swamy temple on the banks of the Kaveri River.
*   **Pratapa Rudra II**, in A.D. 1321, gave donations to the Chenna Keshava swamy temple; his queen **Lakshmidevi** donated gifts to the Ramanatha temple at Elleda.
*   Many **Vishnumurthy temples** were constructed during the Kakatiya period in the Telugu region — at Simhachalam, Sarpavaram, Macherla, Ahobilam, Dharmapuri, Tirupati, Srikurmam, Mangalagiri, Ponnuru, Nelluru, Nandaluru, Kopparam, Karempudi, Kalvakulaku (Mahaboobnagar), Munigadapa, Godaliparti, and Kondapaka (Medak).
*   The **Palanati Veera Charitra** (Battle of Palanadu) also belongs to this period — in reality a war between the followers of the Veervaisnava sect leader **Brahmanaidu** and the Saivite leader **Nayakuralu Nagamma**. **Macherla Chenna Keshavaswamy temple** was a great Vaishnava kshetra of the time; here Brahmanaidu preached casteless, "Jati-less," universal Vaishnavism and organized common dining, known as **"chapakudu."**

Like this, Kakatiya kings respected all religious sects and understood the essence of each, encouraging religious tolerance across their empire (Telangana, Andhra, and Rayalaseema).

Kakatiya kings, ministers, and officials put in great effort for the development of **Sanskrit and Telugu**. Educational institutions and scholars are referenced in period inscriptions.

*   The **A.D. 1261 Malakapuram inscription** describes the conditions of educational buildings and their activities. 

*   **Visveshvara Sivacharya**, Rajaguru to both Ganapatideva and Rudramadevi, received the village Mandaram as an agrahara from Rudramadevi, built a new village named Golaki there, established a Saiva matha, and constructed a **Vidya mandapa** (educational building) where the **Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda, Grammar, Logic, and Literature** were taught. Srisailam and Pushpagiri were other centres with Vidya mandapas. Teaching largely took place in Sanskrit.

*   **Vidyanatha**, Pratapa Rudra II's court poet, was a great Sanskrit poet; his famous work is **"Pratapa­rudriyam"** or **"Pratapa­rudra Yashobhushanam."** **Shalakyamalla kavi** was another great poet of the period, author of "Udaatha raghavam" and "Neeroshte Ramayanam." Rudradeva's Uttareshvara inscription mentions **Viddanacharya**, author of "Prameyacharchamrutam" — a work not available today.
*   Vidyanatha, in his work, praised his emperor Pratapa Rudra II in Alankara shastra, describing his conquests over Kalinga, Pandya, and Seuna (Yadava). 

*   Another popular Sanskrit scholar at Pratapa Rudra II's court was **Gundayabhattu**, who wrote a commentary on Sri Harsha's advaita work _Khandana khanda khadyam_. 
*   **Jayapa**, of the Ayyavamsha, was appointed by Ganapatideva as Gajasahini and wrote **"Nrityaratnavalli"**, describing all the dance and drama forms existing in "Anadhradesa" during the period — it has eight prakarnas (chapters) and remains a standard textbook for dance and drama teachers today; on the walls of the Palampet Ramappa temple, the postures described in this book are carved in detail. 
*   Jayapa senani is also said to have written "Geetaratnavalli" (on music) and "Vaadyaratnavalli" (on musical instruments), though these are not available today.

### Telugu Literature

Telugu's evolution began with words in the _Gaathasaptashati_ of the Satavahana period, and it evolved fully by the Eastern Chalukya period. In the Kakatiya period, as the people of Telangana, Andhra, and Rayalaseema were united, Telugu became popular as **the people's language**; Saiva and Vaishnava poets wrote their works in the local dialect (**Jana Telugu**), and Telugu was used in inscriptions of the period.

Important Telugu poets of this period include **Tikkanna Somayaji, Palkuriki Somanatha, Baddena, Kolanu Ganapatideva, Rudradeva, Ekamaranatha, and Kase Sarvappa**. 

Important Telugu works of the period include **Andhra Mahabharatam, Nirvochanottara Ramayanam, Andhra Dashakumara Charitam, Purushartha saram, Jainendra Kalyanabhyudayam** (Appayyarya was a Jaina poet), **Panditaradya Charitam, Basavapuranam, Sivayoga saram, Neetisaram, Neetisarmuktavalli, Pratapa charitra, Siddeshwara charitra,** and **Kreedhabhi ramam**.

*   **Tikkana Somayaji**, born at Nellore, went to Orugallu and completed his Mahabharata composition at Ganapatideva's court; he is regarded as the figure who culturally unified Telangana-Andhra regions through his literary work, and can be called a foundational figure of the tradition.
*   **Palkuriki Somanatha** wrote works showing that spoken Telugu ("jana Telugu") had no shortage of dignity for poetry; his _Basavapuranam_ develops the life of Veerashaiva reformer Basaveshwara and is not a translation of any Sanskrit work.
*   The dvipada (couplet) literary tradition's most famous work of the era is the **Ranganatha Ramayanam** — its Purva Ramayana portion composed by Buddharaju, and Uttara Ramayana by Vithaladevudu and Buddharaju's sons.
*   The **Bhaskara Ramayanam** was composed jointly by five poets — **Mallikarjuna Bhattu, Kumara Rudrudu, Ayyalaryudu, Bhaskarudu, and Hulakki Bhaskarudu.**
*   Other notable works of the era: **Marana's Markandeya Puranam**, and **Manchana's Keyura Bahu Charitra**.

**Poet Molla** episode (from Social Conditions section above) reflects the caste tensions of the era around literary patronage. Poet **Palkuriki Somanatha** is particularly noted for using vernacular Telugu, freed from excessive Sanskritized vocabulary, while still drawing on earlier Sanskrit source material for many of his ideas.

concepts.partName: Architecture and Monuments of the Kakatiya Period
concepts.bodyMd:
As successors of the Rashtrakutas and Kalyana Chalukyas, the Kakatiyas built wonderful temples, forts, and entrance doors (Toranas) across Telangana and Andhra. Their feudatories, ministers, army chiefs, and regional rulers, inspired by their overlords, also built many beautiful temples.

**Forts:** Forts built during the Kakatiya period include **Golkonda, Orugallu, Deverakonda, Rachakonda, and Bhuvanagiri**, among others.

*   The **Orugallu fort** was particularly strongly built for the protection of the capital, with **three walls**: the **first wall** was constructed of mud, about ten feet high, surrounding Kazipeta and Anumakonda; the **second wall**, also a mud fort, lay outside the Orugallu fort and originally had four entrances on four sides at important points (today only the old city remains within this mud fort). 
*   Passing through this, at a distance of about a furlong, is the **masonry fort**, called **Kanchu Kota** (Bronze fort). Inside this fort stands the temple of **Swayambhunatha**, in front of which four wonderful Toranas (entrance arches) were constructed. The sculptural art of this temple was largely destroyed during the Muslim attacks.

### Temples of the Kakatiya Period and Their Characteristics

Important art and architectural characteristics of Kakatiya temples: (1) high Adhisthana (plinth), (2) pillars with many sculptures, (3) wall parapits of mandapas with Jalies (lattice/checker screens), (4) entrance (Torana) pillars, (5) high vimanas, (6) Ranga mandapas, (7) Mukha mandapas.

**Temple table:**

| Temple | Location | Key details |
|---|---|---|
| Anumakonda thousand-pillar temple (Rudreshwaralayam) | Rudradeva built, A.D. 1163 | A Trikutalaya, with Rudra, Vasudeva, and Surya as main deities; the temple's A.D. 1163 inscription supports the Kakatiyas' declaration of sovereignty |
| Ramappa temple (Rudreshwaralayam) | Palampet village, Mulugu tq., Warangal district, built A.D. 1213 by Ganapatideva's general Recherla Rudradeva | Built on a 6.5 ft upa pitha with a four-storeyed vimana and doors on three sides; features an interior Nandi, decorated tiles, and bold sculptures — including "Madanika" female figures in tri-bhangima poses (per Jayapasenani's Nrityaratnavalli), musician and bhakti-singer carvings, and Rangamandapa pillar scenes of Gopika vasthrapaharanam and rasa kreeda |
| Ghanapuram Fort temple | Warangal | Beautiful Nayika (heroine) sculptures in the Rangamandapa; Nayikas carved in various poses playing musical instruments; Nandi sculpture decorated with a beaded garland |
| Nagulapadu Trikutalayam (1234), Kameshwaralayam (A.D. 1256) | Nagulapadu | Rangamandapam has beautifully carved pillars depicting scenes of the Ravana sabha |
| Swayambhulinga temple (A.D. 1254) | Warangal fort | Destroyed during Muslim attacks; currently in a dilapidated condition |
| Pillalamarri Erekeshwaralayam (A.D. 1208) | Nalgonda | Mukkanteeshwaralayam (A.D. 1195), Nameshwaralayam (A.D. 1203) |
| Soumyanathalayam | Nandaluru | Sculpture of Visvaksena carved in a wonderful way |
| Pachala Someshwaralayam | Panugallu, Nalgonda | Built A.D. 1015–1042, Kalyana Chalukya period |
| Ramlingeshwaralayam | Nandikandi, Medak district | Built A.D. 1015–1042 |

**Significance of temples in medieval society:** Temples in medieval India functioned as landlord, owner, consumer of goods and services, banker, school, museum, and theatre — a centre of excellence in arts and civilization, and a model and instrument of righteous human values.

*   Under Kakatiya patronage, temples in Andhradesa flourished with abundant income and wealth. Ekamranatha's _Pratapa Charitra_ records that in Pratapa Rudra II's kingdom there were **5,500 Saiva temples, 1,300 Vaishnava temples**, 2,400 temples of Mallaradeve, and **4,400 temples** together dedicated to Bhairava, Durga, and Ganapati.
*   The **Srisailam Mallikarjuna Swamy temple** had **fifty-two villages** assigned to it by A.D. 1313 (Pratapa Rudradeva's time), whose income supported daily poojas and services by temple employees and priests. Different castes and traders donated shares of their income to temples; temple lands received special tax exemption. 
*   The **Perikas** (transporters), who carried daily-needed fruits and goods on bulls and bullock carts to various temples, were exempted from tax on these goods — recorded in the Tripuranthakam inscription.

**Sculptural themes:** In Kakatiya sculpture, four broad categories predominate: deity forms, dance forms (Nartaki), dancer groups (Nartakibrundam), and general/secular forms.

Among decorative motifs unconnected to deity forms, six types were prominent: **makara toranas (crocodile-arch motifs), hamsas (swans), padmas (lotuses), latas (creepers/vines), elephants, and lion friezes.** Kakatiya hamsa (swan) motifs are depicted in graceful rows, with wings turned and elaborate feather-patterns forming beautiful borders. 

Kakatiya sculptors gave special importance to elephants and makaras (crocodile-motifs), but — unlike other South Indian temple traditions — rarely carved lions or horses. Sculptors of the period developed a distinctive individual style, producing innumerable variations on traditional themes rather than repeating a single standard pattern.

The **Ramappa temple at Palampet**, Warangal district, is considered the most artistically accomplished of all Kakatiya temples — an example of the Kakatiyas' devotion to the art of dance, built by Recherla Rudradeva (general and minister under Ganapatideva) in A.D. 1213. Every part of the temple is an exquisite work of sculptural art.

*   It is believed that Jayapa Senani himself assisted in perfecting these dance sculptures. The **Nandi at Ramappagudi** is considered an unmatched divine sculptural masterpiece, and the beauty and grace of the carved serpent figures (Nagini) and dance postures there are especially notable.

Devalaya (temple) construction proceeded vigorously throughout the Kakatiya period, and the architectural design skill of Telugu craftsmen flowed generously onto the fine-grained black stone of the region. Kakatiya temples were generally **Trikuta** (three-shrine) constructions — a common feature was that alongside the main temple there would typically be two smaller subsidiary temples. The main shrine was generally dedicated to Shiva, while the subsidiary ones were dedicated to other deities.
